function.name: get_current_weather
function.description: Retrieve the current weather conditions for a specified location in either Celsius or Fahrenheit. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

location.description: The location for which to retrieve the weather, in the format of 'City, State', such as 'San Francisco, CA' or 'New York, NY'.

unit.description: The unit of measurement for the temperature.

function.name: search_local_docs
function.description: Searches the local knowledge base for documents that match the given natural language query and returns relevant document entries. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

query.description: The search query expressed in natural language, such as 'What are the symptoms of a cold?'.

limit.description: The maximum number of documents to return.

include_metadata.description: Determines whether to include metadata for the documents in the search results.

**First Studio Ghibli film to win the Japan Academy Film Prize for Picture of the Year** | Year of Award | Ceremony | Winning Film | Notes | |---------------|----------|--------------|-------| | 1998 | 21st Japan Academy Prize (for films released in 1997) | **“Princess Mononoke”** | This was the first time a Studio Ghibli feature received the top honor at the Japan Academy Film Prize. | *“Princess Mononoke”* (released in Japan on July 12 1997) earned the Picture‑of‑the‑Year award at the 21st ceremony, beating out other strong contenders such as *“The Last Emperor”* and *“The Wind Rises”* (the latter would win in 2004). --- ### How its box‑office success boosted Ghibli’s international profile | Domestic Impact | International Impact | |-----------------|----------------------| | • Grossed **¥1.5 billion** (≈ US$15 million) in Japan, making it one of the highest‑grossing Japanese animated films of the decade.
• Became the highest‑grossing film in Japan for 1997, surpassing *“The Last Emperor”* and *“The Lion King”*. | • Distributed in the United States by **Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures** (under the “Disney–Ghibli” label).
• Earned **US$13 million** in the U.S. market, a record for a foreign‑language animated feature at the time.
• The film’s success proved that Ghibli’s storytelling could resonate with Western audiences, encouraging Disney to acquire distribution rights for other Ghibli titles (*“My Neighbor Totoro”*, *“Kiki’s Delivery Service”*, *“Spirited Away”*, etc.). | | • The film’s critical acclaim (winning the Picture‑of‑the‑Year award) reinforced its domestic prestige, leading to a surge in home‑video sales and television broadcasts. | • The partnership with Disney opened the door to a broader international release strategy, including subtitled/dubbed versions in Europe, Australia, and later in Asia.
• The film’s success helped build a global fanbase that would later support the worldwide acclaim of *“Spirited Away”* (which won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature in 2003). | | • The film’s popularity spurred merchandise sales, theme‑park attractions, and a dedicated fan community within Japan. | • The international box‑office performance demonstrated that Ghibli’s high‑quality animation and mature themes could compete with Hollywood blockbusters, giving the studio leverage in negotiating future distribution deals (e.g., Netflix’s 2019 agreement to stream all Ghibli films). | **Bottom line:** *Princess Mononoke*’s domestic triumph and its record‑breaking U.S. run proved that Studio Ghibli could produce commercially viable, critically acclaimed films that appealed to both Japanese and Western audiences. This dual success laid the groundwork for Ghibli’s subsequent international expansion, turning the studio into a globally recognized powerhouse of animation.
